45.7% (32/70) of non-MPR patients have high Texp cell levels (Texp.in.Tex.relevant*10 > 8.05, the within-non-MPR median split threshold). 95% CI: 34.6% to 57.3%. (6 patients, 8.6%, could not be classified due to missing Texp data.)

These high-Texp non-MPR patients have recurrence-free survival statistically indistinguishable from pathological responders (MPR patients): 12-month RFS 90.2% vs 95.2%, 24-month RFS 86.4% vs 88.6%, log-rank p = 0.635, Cox HR = 1.32 (95% CI 0.41-4.28, p = 0.65). In contrast, low-Texp non-MPR patients have dramatically worse outcomes: 12-month RFS 58.2%, 24-month RFS 41.6%, median RFS 15.78 months, with a 7.7-fold higher recurrence hazard vs MPR (HR 7.73, 95% CI 3.43-17.44, p < 0.001) and an 83% lower hazard in high vs low Texp non-MPR (HR 0.17, 95% CI 0.06-0.51, p = 0.001).

Thus, nearly half of non-MPR patients harbor high Texp levels and enjoy RFS comparable to pathological responders, despite lacking a pathological response — identifying Texp as a candidate biomarker that reclassifies radiological non-responders into a favorable-prognosis subgroup.
